'''''Trifolium alexandrinum''''' ('''Egyptian clover''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=Egyptian Clover ''Trifolium alexandrinum'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.hgf | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref> '''berseem clover''')<ref>{{GRIN |accessdate=26 April 2011}}</ref> is a species of [[clover]]. The plant can reach {{cvt|75|cm}} tall, with [[trifoliate]] leaves and whitish flowers. It is native to [[northeast Africa]] and [[southwest Asia]].

== Description ==
The [[annual plant]] reaches {{cvt|45 to 75|cm}} tall with erect or ascending stems, the growth habit resembling [[Trifolium pratense|red clover]]. The leaves are [[trifoliate]], with slender leaflets. The flowers are white to creamy white, produced in inflorescences similar to those of [[Trifolium repens|white clover]] with around 100 flowers.<ref name="FAO">{{cite book |url=https://www.fao.org/3/a-i3500e.pdf |last1=Muhammad |first1=Dost |last2=Misri |first2=Bimal |last3=El-Nahrawy |first3=Mohamed |last4=Khan |first4=Sartaj |last5=Serkan |first5=Ates |title=Egyptian clover (Trifolium alexandrinum) |publisher=FAO Regional Office for the Near East and North Africa |location=Cairo |date=2014 |isbn=9785-108008-5-92}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is native to northeast Africa and southwest Asia, from Egypt east to Pakistan.<ref name="522827-1">{{cite POWO |id=522827-1 |title=''Trifolium alexandrinum'' L. |access-date=28 April 2022 }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Egyptian clover is cultivated mostly in irrigated sub-tropical regions, and used as leguminous crop. It is an important winter crop in Egypt, where it may have been cultivated since ancient times,<ref name="FAO"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://aces.nmsu.edu/pubs/docs/Egyptian%20clover%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf |title=USAID Fact Sheet: Berseem Clover |last=Oushy |first=Hamdy |date=2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121115143400/https://aces.nmsu.edu/pubs/docs/Egyptian%20clover%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf|archive-date=2012-11-15}}</ref> and was introduced into northern India in the early nineteenth century. It is also grown in northern Africa west of its native range, and in Australia, China, Europe and the United States,<ref name="522827-1"/> and is locally [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] north to England.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>

There are two agricultural [[cultivar group]]s of berseem clover, single-cut and multi-cut. Single-cut [[cultivar]]s, like 'Balady', feature a high growing point and have poor recovery once harvested. Multi-cut cultivars, like 'Frosty', feature a lower growing point allowing for multiple harvests from a single sowing.

It is generally frost-sensitive and should be planted only after potential for frost has passed. The exception is 'Frosty' berseem clover which was developed by [[Grassland]] Oregon, Inc. and released in 2016. This variety is capable of surviving temperatures as low as {{cvt|5|F|C|order=flip}}.<ref>{{Cite press release |url=https://agnewswire.com/2018/01/16/cold-tolerant-berseem-clover-provides-frost-seeding-option/ |title=Cold Tolerant Berseem Clover Provides Frost Seeding Option |date=2018-01-16 |website=AgNewsWire |language=en-US |access-date=2019-07-06}}</ref>

===Forage===
Egyptian clover provides highly nutritious fodder for livestock in winter season in repeated cuttings. Yields range from 44 to 71 tonnes per hectare of forage in a single growing season.<ref name="FAO"/> It contains 17% crude protein, 25.9% crude fibre and 60–65% TDN (Total Digestible Nutrients) content.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dairy Knowledge |url=https://www.dairyknowledge.in/article/berseem#:~:text=Berseem%20is%20highly%20palatable%20fodder,to%20ruminants%20leads%20to%20bloat.}}</ref> Berseem needs a mild temperature to germinate and further establishment. Its growth is restricted during severe cold or frosty weather. It grows well on medium to heavy soils and is tolerant of salinity,<ref name="FAO"/> and is similar in forage quality to [[alfalfa]].<ref name="FAO"/>

===Green manure===
Egyptian clover can also be used as a [[cover crop]] suppressing weeds or as a green manure crop providing nitrogen to following crops. As a [[green manure]] crop, berseem is capable of providing from 300-400 kg/ha of nitrogen to following crops.<ref name="FAO"/>
